text:
Sry to hear about that. I get the same spam commenting here sometimes and it's really not his fault. JayzTwoCents doesn't control youtube spammers or youtube and he can't clean the comments up himself. He has made a video warning people about this in the past, tried to bring it to youtube's attention and so on and so forth. Unfortunately he can't do much about it. It's out of his control and it's not possible to warn everyone every time, because it's just constant "You have won. Contact us." spam. So what can be done? Do you think they should put a disclaimer at the end of every video, like "please read names carefully and check who you are replying to, because I am not JayZtwoCents or JayzTwoCentsOfficial or JayzTwoCentsonTelegram or or or" and it's not just him either. This happens across a lot of big channels and nobody has a disclaimer. It's a youtube problem. You gotta be really careful and make sure you are reading the names and comparing them to that of the channel. If they don't match, chances are you aren't talking to who you think you are talking to. So again, sry to hear you were scammed, but it absolutely wasn't this channel that scammed you. By the way, I am not a verified account or channel owner, just some dude, a fellow youtube user. 

It's kind of like reading your credit card info out to the "Microsoft Support" guys that will call you at home. Microsoft can't go around and find everyone that gets contacted to warn them, that their support will not just randomly call people to fix some invented issue. Nor can they make you check carefully where emails you receive come from or police what you do with your account data, logins, bank info etc. So it really really sucks, that it happened to you, but at the end of the day no channel owner is responsible for your actions, you are.

text:
Electrical engineer here. I believe I know why your performance kept dropping at higher voltages. If I'm correct, it may also be implicated with some of the crashing that people have been seeing. 

TL;DR: The GPU core is current limited (not necessarily by the VRM). Increasing core voltage makes this much worse. 

The job of Buck converter (1 stage VRM) is to step voltage down efficiently. However, conservation of energy applies.
If the power into a 3090's VRM is 350 Watts and it is 90% efficient, it can only supply about 315 Watts to the core. At 950 mV, that means the VRM is limited to output 332.5 Amps to the core.
Now, take the Titan RTX with a 280 Watt power limit at a GPU Voltage of 0.96 (GamersNexus review article). With the same 90% VRM efficiency, the power supplied is 252 Watts. At 960 mV, this corresponds to 262.5 Amps to the core. 
Due to architectural differences, Ampere has at LEAST 1.25x the number of transistors per CUDA core (on average, see AdoredTV's CUDA Evolution video). Factoring in the CUDA core count increase from 4608 to 10496, a CONSERVATIVE estimate for the total increase in transistor count due to CUDA cores is ~2.85x. Current supplied by the VRM should increase proportionally with CUDA transistor count, since most of the energy is used by the core. This means, given NO node shrink, we could expect the 3090 core to pull over 2.85x the current from the VRM when all CUDA cores are fully loaded. 
This poses a bit of a problem, since the shrink to Samsung 8nm wouldn't have even reduced current draw by 2x. Even if we do assume 2x, then feeding current to all of those cores would take ~373 Amps from the VRM. As a result, at 350 Watts and 950 mV, the 3090 needs 12% more current to fully utilize its 10490 CUDA cores. Increasing the voltage just decreases the current, since Current = Power / Voltage. If you want to feed these GPUs, you need to really find the sweet spot for voltage. Increasing it will decrease your usable cores at high frequencies while decreasing it may reduce stability.

text:
10900k or 3950x are both useless for SLI in my opinion. Especially on the long run when games become more demanding and thus more data is being swapped between (at a certain point in time limited) video ram and system ram. At which point you will want and need full 16x PCI 4.0 speeds for each cards or they will get bottlenecked.

Reviewers always like to have a dick contest when hardware is new and benchmark everything on a fresh system, but that is not how Joe Average is going to use his computer.

So I take all the bla bla with a grain of salt, but it gives me a rough real world performance guess. So I still watch a couple to get a coarse idea of the products used and their limitations.

text:
if you knew as much as you let on you would know that SLI/crossfire is a gimmick and not practical for the end-user. And you wouldn't be making videos like these in 2020. You and i both know you will get better performance using a single graphics card. Another youtuber pretending to care about the end-user NOT (prob paid to perpetuate the gimmick that is SLI)

SLI/CFX costs twice the money, consumes twice the power, clutters your case twice as much, but NEVER gives twice the performance. In fact it trashes frame latency. Using two videocards is like having two guns but only one gun barrel and they both have to take turns firing rounds. DX12 was supposed to remedy this by giving each card its own cpu core but DX12 never materialized. So anyone using cfx/sli is a simp. And jayz might possibly not make it into heaven now for keeping sli/cfx alive

if you are just a gamer. Spend a bit more on a single powerful card. Every single person ive ever known to buy two videocards at once has one unplugged and gathering dust within about 30 days. Dont DO IT

@JayzTwoCents turn your bench on it's side and blow in directly at the motherboard. Basically you want to eliminate laminar airflow and this will help do that. I use 1200cfm blower fans during the winter at night to do heavy overclocking at around 40-50f and they just sit with the side panel off of the case and it's fine. Even during the summer it's absolutely fine while running folding@home. If you're blowing so much air that it's creating a vacuum at the card you need to get the card to a positive air pressure so that the fans can suck air in even if the AC is blowing on them so fast it would otherwise suck the air away. If you do this so that the AC is creating turbulence near the card where the air has nowhere to go except through the fan this should fix the issues you're having. The reason paul's shroud worked well was because it hit his setup at a 45 degree angle which helped disrupt the laminar airflow, creating turbulence in between the 2 cards and next to the 2nd card both. he showed his boost clocks were consistent and high with that setup. If I had the budget and my studio was fully built I'd enter the ring and prove this right myself (for I too have a floor standing window AC!) but since you're the only one having trouble I figured I'd write it all out for you and see if that helps. If this fixes your problems just give me a shout out in the video. Haven't launched my channel yet but it's gonna be called DJPC Tech. Hope all this helps, good luck! 

edit: I want to add that if your card has a vertical fin design (fins open at the top going through the length of the card) that this will also force air directly through the cooler, potentially moving more air than you could ever push through with just the fans on the card. Basically all my folding@home cards are like this for that reason

The cards that go out to reviewers (which enables reviewers to do their job) don't affect the stock that is on the market for the general public. On the bright side, by the time we normies get a chance to buy a card, drivers will be a bit more mature, some issues will be worked out and we will also get to see what the competition is doing. So really, waiting a few months is generally better for us as consumers than being early adopters 🙂.

text: Hey Jay, the way you have it setup at 14:15 you might be creating what’s called a Venturi, essentially what’s happening is as your blowing fast air across the rear of the card it creates a vacuum and will choke off airflow to the fans. Carburetors use this Venturi principle to add fuel to the air mixture. The faster you blow air over an aperture, the higher the amount of fluid (in the case of a Carburetor it’s gasoline) will be sucked out of that aperture. However since air is our fluid in our test bench, the fans simply can’t keep up with the velocity of air blowing across the backside of the graphics cards. Think of it as running lean for a car engine!! It will run hot because you don’t have enough “fuel” in our mixture. I hope this makes sense! A simple experiment you can do is you get a cup of water and a straw, then simply blow air over the top of the straw where you would take a sip. You’ll see water come out the straw!

text:
@ironroad18  All words are made up. But "bottleneck" comes from the neck of a bottle. If you pour water out of a bottle, the neck slows it down. If you break the neck off and pour the water out, it comes out way faster. That's the concept of a bottleneck. It's not so much a buzzword as it is a reality.

In the space of PCs, a bottleneck is one part of your system acting like the neck of a bottle; it's limiting something somewhere that would allow it to achieve maximum performance. Example: put a 3090 in a pentium 3 machine and see the FPS; it's going to perform worse than a modern CPU with low-mid GPU. So, it's effectively acting like a bottleneck, or, ahem, bottlenecking the performance.

text:
I assume you're joking, based on the ":P" part. If you're not... just.. no. If you rounded up every reviewer that actually got sent a card, you're maybe looking at 30-40 cards total that were sent out to influencers/reviews. They didn't ship only 50 cards across the rest of the world, it was thousands upon thousands. But almost none of these cards were part of the stock shipped out to the public. They go from the AIB straight to the influencer/reviewer. 

So they have little to no effect on the availability of a product that is being produced in bulk now; and just has to leave the factories in Asia to the retailers in the rest of the world.
author: @ExarchGaming

text: @ExarchGaming  Obviously I am joking, but half joking.  Do we even know how many 3090s made it to the wild?  40 cards just to do SLI videos where only .000001% of 3090 owners are going to do seems kind of meh when cards are in SUCH limited supply, yes?
author: @rikachiu

text:
@rikachiu  Not really, no? These cards were not from the stock going to consumers, they're sent directly from the AIB to the reviewer. 40 cards is a generous estimate tbh, the amount that were sent out were likely in much more limited quantities. 

We know that all of the AIBs are in full production mode for their cards, and they are flowing in to stores, Lets say Nvidia did a very limited run of cards, 1,000. (these are founders editions) they sent out 1 or 2 to some reviewers. People like UFD Tech I don't believe got one, among several others. Many reviewers had to buy their own card. 

So, lets go with that completely completely generous estimate of 40 cards being sent out to reviewers (from FE) that's 4 percent, 96 percent were either bought by lucky early adopters, or snapped up by bot-laden scalpers. 

Now, they're getting a bunch of AIB cards, MSI, Gigabyte, Asus, EVGA ect. They're shipping these cards out as fast as they can make them. If you go to Gamers Nexus, you can see I believe how they're made, or at least how extensive  the production factories are that produce hardware. 

The reason week 1 was so hard, was the AIBs were given absolutely no time to fully test their cards, so that caused a bit of a delay, that's nvidia's fault. 

Infact you can go to Nvidia's website where they address the issue. They had great supply, and their cards are in full production, and have been since august. That gives a potential for thousands or tens of thousands. 

People who think that influencers or reviewers have any impact on the global supply of these cards are naive, in the most literal way. The world isn't limited to just what you read, or who you know. know what I mean?
author: @ExarchGaming

text:
@ExarchGaming  I get it, but there were more than 40 people who wanted this card, me included.  According to Bit Wit's video, you had people lining up DAYS ahead of time for 26 cards at the one microcenter in the largest state in the US.  

So doing something so decadent as SLIing 3090s during such a shortage is kind of meh.

author: @ExarchGaming

text:
@rikachiu  I'm sure, but blame the people who sucked up the 96 percent, not the 4 percent. You mention 26 cards in kyle's video(which i referenced as well) but quantify that with california being the largest state in the US (by population I assume, not size; as Texas and Alaska are larger by a significant margin) 

That one microcenter wasn't the only location in all of california to have supply though, just the closest one to Kyle. There are other retailers that were given supply as well. Microcenter certainly wasn't the only exclusive location to feature the Ampere Cards. 

As i pointed out in my last comment, Nvidia addressed all of this; they have been in full production since august. That is a lot of cards. 

Just to put a number to that, PC Partner can produce 400,000 graphics cards every month, 4000 per day. You understand why people thinking that influencers/reviews affect global supply is silly...right? 


As per your last response, I don't know how to answer that. Someone having something I want to buy, and me not being able to get it doesn't really affect me much. I'm building a new rig right now, have been saving money for a year and some change. I decided to wait for Zen 3/RDNA 2 and Ampere. No one "needs" one of these right now. It's a luxury item, so I think people getting legitimately upset at influencers specifically for having these cards while they don't, are being childish at best.

text:
you need an SLI bridge which allows you to install the 2 cards not side by side, but staggered with the fans pointing to opposite direction. 
so 1 card with the HDMI port pointing to the right , the second card pointing to the left. the fans pointing to the outside 
so 1 card will pull air from the top, the other from the bottom but the hot air between the 2 cards will never go inside the fans of the 2nd card.

or... ask MSI to create a special 3090 SLI card, with in inversed PCB... all the components (gpu, ram, heatsink...) moved to the opposite side of the PCB.
in this case, the card can be setup in a standard case
